Content: ... Before those grim visions [global hunger] could come to pass, the green revolution transformed global agriculture, especially wheat and rice. Through selective breeding, Norman Borlaug, an American biologist, created a dwarf variety of wheat that put most of its energy into edible kernels rather than long, inedible stems. The result: more grain `text(per acre)`. Similar work at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) in the Philippines dramatically improved the productivity of the grain that feeds nearly `text(half)` the world.

From the `text(1960s)` through the `text(1990s)`, yields of rice and wheat in Asia `text(doubled)`. Even as the continent's population increased by `text(60 percent)`, grain prices fell, the average Asian consumed nearly a `text(third)` more calories, and the poverty rate was cut in `text(half)`. When Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize in `1970`, the citation read, “More than any other person of this age, he helped provide bread for a hungry world.” ...
